passage: By August, Layla had worked eleven weeks at the bakery by the harbour, long enough to know who closed up properly. Ana did: counted the till, wiped the ovens, never left early. So when the owner announced the new shift-lead job, Layla expected Ana's name. It was Diego's. Diego, the son of the owner's oldest friend, came in late on Saturdays with sand still on his shoes. Ana just nodded and went back to the dough. Later the owner told Layla, a little embarrassed, "His mother helped me open this place. He's practically family." Layla could picture that, and it softened her; she'd want to help someone like that too. But walking home she kept seeing Ana's floury hands, and eleven weeks of good work that hadn't counted.

qa.q: Who did Layla expect to be named shift lead?
qa.a: Layla expected Ana's name.

qa.q: Why did the owner's explanation soften Layla, even briefly?
qa.a: Layla felt sympathy for that loyalty to an old friend's family and knew she might feel the same pull herself.

qa.q: What could Layla choose to do now about the unfairness she saw?
qa.a: Layla could tell Ana that the careful work was noticed, and later suggest the owner choose shift leads by clear duties.

qa.q: How might Ana see the decision, going back to the dough without a word?
qa.a: Ana may feel that eleven weeks of careful work counted for less than a family tie, and may quietly stop going the extra mile.

grounding: A student worker sees a family friend's son promoted over a harder worker, understanding the pull of loyalty but also the unfairness.

passage: The nomination desk closed at four. Jaya, volunteering in the college office, had turned away two students at 4:05, one of them in tears. At 4:40 Gautam strolled in with his form. Professor Rane, in charge of the election, looked up and smiled. "Gautam! How is your father? Tell him Sunday lunch is on." The form went into the pile. Jaya's pen stopped. She knew the two families had holidayed together for years; she'd seen the photos on the office wall. Part of her understood: you look after your own, you don't shame them in public. But she had said no to a crying girl barely half an hour earlier. That evening she wrote a short, polite email to the student council, asking that late forms be handled the same way for everyone.

qa.q: At what time did Gautam bring in his form?
qa.a: Gautam strolled in at 4:40, after the desk had closed at four.

qa.q: What was Jaya thinking when her pen stopped?
qa.a: She partly understood the professor's loyalty to a family friend, but felt it was unfair after she had turned away a crying girl.

qa.q: Jaya chose a polite email to the council over confronting the professor. What makes that a sensible choice?
qa.a: It raises the fairness problem through the proper channel and asks for one rule for everyone, without a public scene.

qa.q: How might the two students turned away at 4:05 feel if they learned about Gautam's form?
qa.a: They would likely feel cheated, seeing the rule applied strictly to them but bent for someone with the right family connection.

grounding: A student at the election desk sees a family friend's son allowed a late nomination, and weighs the pull of loyalty against fairness.

passage:
Dear Kiran,
You asked how the internship at the insurance office is going. Mostly fine. But something happened that I can't stop thinking about.
They were hiring one junior clerk. Two people interviewed: a woman from the evening college who answered every question sharply, and Harpreet veerji, whose family and mine have celebrated every Lohri together since before I was born. The branch head is his father's old friend. Harpreet got the job the same afternoon.
I was happy for him for about ten minutes. I even texted Mum. Then I saw the other candidate at the bus stop, reading her notes again. She didn't know yet.
I understand why it happened. If it were my own brother, would I want someone to help? Probably yes. That's what bothers me.
Write back and tell me what you'd have done.
Baljeet

qa.q: How long have Baljeet's family and Harpreet's celebrated Lohri together?
qa.a: Since before Baljeet was born.

qa.q: Why does "Probably yes" bother Baljeet so much?
qa.a: Baljeet feels uncomfortable realising the same pull toward one's own people is inside Baljeet too, which makes it hard to simply condemn what happened.

qa.q: If Baljeet is ever the one hiring, what choice would respect both loyalty and fairness?
qa.a: Baljeet could help a relative prepare or hear about openings, while leaving the decision itself to an equal, fair interview.

qa.q: What might the other candidate at the bus stop feel when she hears the news?
qa.a: She may feel her sharp answers never had a real chance, and she might lose trust in how that office hires.

grounding: A student intern sees a family friend hired over a stronger candidate and recognises both the pull of loyalty and the harm to fairness.

passage: "Zainab, it's me, Aditi, the girl who can't keep quiet. Can I tell you something weird about my coaching centre job? I just file papers there part-time. Last week they needed a new maths teacher for the evening batch. Two people gave demo classes. One was a woman who'd taught for five years; the kids actually clapped at the end of her demo. The other was Rohit, the owner's nephew, who mumbled and got a sum wrong. The owner gave it to Rohit. I heard him tell his wife, 'He's family. His father helped me when I had nothing.' And honestly, a part of me understood that. If my Chacha was struggling, I'd want to help him too. But then I saw the kids in Rohit's class, bored, confused, and I thought of that other teacher. Families look after their own. But those kids are paying for it, and so is she."

qa.q: What did the students do at the end of the experienced teacher's demo?
qa.a: The kids actually clapped at the end of her demo.

qa.q: What mixed feelings does Aditi have about the owner's choice?
qa.a: Aditi understands the pull to help family, since she would want to help her own Chacha, but is troubled by the harm to the students and the better teacher.

qa.q: What could the owner have done to help Rohit without harming the students?
qa.a: He could have hired the better teacher and helped Rohit in another way, such as giving him training or a different role.

qa.q: How are the students in the evening batch affected by the choice?
qa.a: They get a teacher who mumbles and makes mistakes, leaving them bored and confused while paying for the classes.

grounding: A student sees a relative hired over a better candidate and understands the pull of family loyalty while seeing the harm to fairness.

passage: I'm Rashmi, and I play on our college's women's cricket team, so I saw the men's selection from the next net. Samir had been the best opening batsman in the trials all week; he hit the ball cleanly and never lost his wicket cheaply. On Friday the list went up. Samir wasn't on it. Instead there was Karan, who had got out for nothing twice. Everyone knew Karan's uncle and the coach had grown up in the same village and still went to each other's weddings. I don't know what the coach was thinking. Maybe he felt he owed that family. I can even understand that; my own father would do almost anything for his cousins. But I saw Samir's face when he read the list, and then I saw him quietly pack his kit and leave before practice.

qa.q: Who was the best opening batsman in the trials?
qa.a: Samir had been the best opening batsman in the trials all week.

qa.q: What does Samir quietly packing his kit suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he is hurt and discouraged, feeling his good performance did not count against a family connection.

qa.q: What could the college do to keep selection fair?
qa.a: It could publish trial scores and have more than one person on the selection panel, so a single coach's family ties cannot decide.

qa.q: How might Karan feel knowing the reason for the selection?
qa.a: Karan might feel uneasy or less proud of the place in the team, knowing others think it came from family ties rather than batting.

grounding: A student sees a coach pick a relative's family member over a better player, understanding the pull of loyalty while seeing the harm to fairness.
